items.title: The Hardest One To Admit
items.content:
Every other track in this app is about something you did to yourself. This one is about something you did to other people. That's why it's the hardest door to walk through, and why most people never do.

It's easier to say "I have a problem with porn" than "I scare the people I love." The first one makes you a person struggling. The second one makes you the villain in somebody else's story, and nobody volunteers for that. So instead you say you have a temper. You say you're stressed. You say they know how to push your buttons. All of which lets you keep the behavior and skip the reckoning.

Here's the deal for the next thirty days. You're going to look at it straight, without the excuses and without the self-hatred — because both of those are exits. Excuses let you off. Self-hatred feels like accountability but it's actually just another way of making it about your pain instead of theirs. Neither one changes what happens the next time you get to a 9.

What does change it: understanding the mechanics, catching it earlier, and building an exit you actually use. That's learnable. Thousands of people have done it. You showing up here at all puts you ahead of most.

One more thing, said plainly. Anger you can learn to manage. A pattern of controlling or frightening someone is a different problem that needs more than an app — Day 15 covers how to tell which one you've got, and Day 28 covers what to do about it. Read both before you decide you've got this handled.
items.action: Write one sentence with no qualifier attached: "I have ___ and it has hurt ___." No "but." No "because they." Just the sentence.
items.reflection: What's the word you've been using instead of the true one — temper, stress, frustration? What's the true one?

items.title: Anger Is Never The First Feeling
items.content:
Anger is usually a secondary emotion. It arrives second. Something else lands first — and it lands so fast you almost never see it, because anger is louder and faster and feels a hundred times better than what's underneath.

What's underneath is almost always one of a short list: disrespected. Not good enough. Powerless. Afraid. Ashamed. Ignored. Trapped. Notice that every one of those is a small, defenseless feeling. Anger is the fastest way out of sitting in a small, defenseless feeling for even one second. It converts helplessness into power, instantly, at the cost of everyone in the room.

That's why the trigger so rarely fits the explosion. The dish in the sink isn't a dish; it's "nobody in this house respects what I do." The driver who cut you off isn't a driver; they're "I don't matter and everyone gets to push past me." You're never as angry at the thing as you look. You're angry at what the thing meant.

This gives you your first real tool, and it's not a breathing exercise. It's a question: **what did that just mean to me?** Asking it, even after the fact at first, starts building a gap between the trigger and the detonation. That gap is where all of recovery lives.
items.action: Take the last time you blew up. Under it, write the first feeling — the half-second one, before the anger. Disrespected? Afraid? Ashamed?
items.reflection: Which of those small feelings is hardest for you to sit in for even ten seconds?

items.title: Ninety Seconds
items.content:
Here's the physical side, because it explains something you've probably experienced as "I couldn't stop it."

When the switch flips, the body takes over: heart rate up, jaw and fists tight, hearing narrows, vision tunnels. And the thinking part of you — the part that weighs consequences and finds words — gets much harder to reach. You've felt it: at full flood you genuinely cannot find the careful version of the sentence. You're running on older hardware. Judgment is simply further away than it was thirty seconds earlier.

The useful part: many people find the surge itself passes in something like ninety seconds if nothing keeps feeding it. Ninety seconds. What keeps it going past that is you — the replay, the argument in your head, the case you keep building. Left alone, the body tends to come down. Fed, it stays up for hours.

So the whole game is: get to ninety seconds without doing damage. Not "stay calm" — you're past calm. Not "win the argument" — you can't, you're on old hardware. Just get through a minute and a half without a word or a hand leaving your body. Walk. Cold water on your face and wrists. Breathe out longer than you breathe in — many people find the long exhale is what finally tells the body the threat is over.

You're not learning to never get angry. You're learning to be somewhere else for ninety seconds.
items.action: Practice the exhale now, while you're calm: in for 4, out for 8, ten rounds. Practicing it cold is what makes it available hot.
items.reflection: What's the first physical signal you get — jaw, chest, hands, heat in the face? That's your alarm. Do you know it yet?

items.title: Road Rage: A Stranger Who Owes You Nothing
items.content:
Road rage deserves its own lesson because it's the purest sample of the whole problem — no history, no relationship, no real stake. Just you and a stranger and a completely disproportionate response.

A car does three things to a human being. It puts you in a metal box that feels private, so the normal restraints of being seen fall away. It removes every human signal — no face, no voice, no way to read intent — so you fill the blank with the worst interpretation available. And it turns every small event into a status event: they cut in front of me, they're holding me up, that driver thinks they can do that to me. Behind the wheel, ordinary traffic gets read as personal disrespect.

Which tells you what's really going on. If a stranger who can't see you, doesn't know you, and will never affect your life again can put you at a 9 — the 9 was already in you when you got in the car. They didn't create it. They gave it somewhere to go.

And it's the one form of this that can kill people who have nothing to do with your life. That's worth sitting with for a second longer than feels comfortable.

Practical, today: leave earlier than you need to — most of it is time pressure wearing a disguise. Kill the noise. When it starts, say out loud, actually out loud, "that's a stranger and I'm fine." And measure the honest cost: eighteen seconds. That's what tailgating them wins you.
items.action: Next drive: leave 10 minutes early and let one person merge in front of you on purpose. Notice what it costs you. It costs nothing.
items.reflection: What were you already carrying the last time a stranger's driving set you off?

items.title: The People Who Got The Worst Of You
items.content:
Nobody rages at their boss the way they rage at home. Think about what that means, because it's uncomfortable and it's important.

You've been holding it together all day. Traffic, work, disrespect, money, whatever it is — you swallow all of it, because there are consequences out there. Then you walk through your own door, into the one place where the consequences felt survivable, and it comes out on the people who did the least to earn it. Your partner. Your kids. The dog. Whoever's closest and safest.

Which proves something you may not want proven: you have control. You've been exercising it all day long, everywhere else. The rage isn't a switch that flips at random; it's a valve that opens where you've decided it's safe to open it. That's not a comfortable fact. It's also the most hopeful one in this whole track, because a thing you're already doing selectively is a thing you can learn to do everywhere.

And understand what it did to them. They learned to read your face from across a room. They learned to scan your mood before deciding whether to ask you anything. They learned to be small. They may still love you completely and be doing all of that. Both at once.

Nothing here is asking you to hate yourself for it. It's asking you to stop calling it uncontrollable when the evidence of your own workday says otherwise.
items.action: Write the name of the person who has absorbed the most of it. Just the name, and one honest sentence about what it's cost them.
items.reflection: Why is it safe to let go at home? What are you actually counting on from them?

items.title: The Shame Cycle
items.content:
There's a loop that runs after the explosion and it is the engine that keeps the whole thing going.

It goes: blow up. Come down. See their face. Feel the shame arrive like a truck. Then handle the shame the only way you know — get busy, get distant, get drunk, get on the phone, act out, go silent, or go looking for a reason it was their fault. And that leaves the original wreckage unrepaired and a new layer of self-disgust on top, which makes you more brittle, which means the next one comes sooner and bigger.

Guilt and shame aren't the same thing and the difference decides everything. Guilt says *I did a bad thing* — it points at the behavior, it hurts, and it produces repair. Shame says *I am a bad thing* — it points at you, it's unbearable, and it produces escape. Every time you escape, you skip repair. Skipping repair is what turns bad nights into a bad decade.

Watch how shame protects the behavior. "I'm a monster" sounds like harsh honesty. It's actually a way to make the moment about your suffering rather than theirs — and a person drowning in self-hatred has no capacity left to go apologize properly.

So the discipline is boring and unglamorous: after it happens, you don't get to spiral and you don't get to disappear. You come back, you own the specific thing, you repair what you can, you get on with the day. Guilt, used, then set down.
items.action: After the next slip — no spiral, no vanishing act. Fifteen minutes, then go back into the room and own the specific thing you did.
items.reflection: What do you reach for after an outburst? Be honest. That's the second half of the loop.

items.title: Week One: Not A Monster. Still Your Job.
items.content:
Six days in, hold two things at the same time, because dropping either one is how people fail at this.

One: you're not a monster. Almost everybody with this problem learned it somewhere — a house where anger was the only permitted emotion, or the only one that got results, or a parent who taught you exactly this by demonstration. There are real mechanics behind it: the secondary emotion, the ninety seconds, the safe valve, the shame loop. Those explain a lot.

Two: none of that is a defense. Not one word of it changes what your kids saw or what your partner learned to expect. Explanation is for you, so you can fix it. It is never for them, and it should never be handed to them as currency. The moment "I had a rough childhood" becomes a sentence you say to the person you just frightened, you've turned understanding into a weapon.

People fail this in two directions. Some take the explanation and stop there — I know why I do it, so now everyone should be patient. Others take the accountability and drown in it — I'm garbage, no point trying. The narrow road between those is the only one that goes anywhere: I understand it, it's mine, I'm working it, and the work is measured in what other people experience, not in how bad I feel.

Next week is mechanics. Triggers, the ladder, the exit — the actual tools.
items.action: Say it out loud once: "I know where it came from. It's still mine to fix." Both halves. Neither one alone.
items.reflection: Which side do you fall off — the excuse side or the self-hatred side?

items.title: Map Your Triggers
items.content:
"It comes out of nowhere" is never true. It comes out of the same three or four places every time, and you've never written them down, so it keeps feeling like weather instead of a pattern.

There are two kinds and you need both. **Situations** — the specific ones: being interrupted, being told you're wrong in front of someone, being ignored when you're talking, running late, money conversations, being told to calm down, a mess after you cleaned, someone questioning how you did something. **States** — the conditions that lower the bar: tired, hungry, hungover, behind at work, in pain, coming down off something, or having already swallowed three things earlier that day.

Here's the multiplier that catches people out: the same situation that's a 2 on a good day is a 9 when you're running on four hours of sleep and skipped lunch. Nothing about the trigger changed. Everything about your capacity did. Which means half of this work isn't done in the moment at all — it's done at 6am, by not arriving at 6pm empty.

Write the list. Not vague — specific. "Disrespect" is useless. "Being corrected in front of my kids" is a thing you can see coming, plan for, and warn people about.
items.action: Write your top 5 situations and your top 3 states. Keep it in the app's Journal. Add to it every time one surprises you.
items.reflection: Which one shows up most? Could you have predicted your last three blowups from this list?

items.title: The Ladder
items.content:
The mistake almost everyone makes is trying to stop it at the top. At a 9 you have no tools — the words and the judgment are gone, that's what a 9 is. The work happens on the way up, and to work it, you have to be able to feel the rungs.

Build your own scale, 1 to 10, with an actual physical marker for each. It'll be personal, but it looks something like: 3 — jaw tightens, I go quiet. 5 — heat in my chest, I start rehearsing what I'm about to say. 6 — voice gets flat and short. 7 — I'm interrupting, standing up, moving toward. 8 — volume, and I stop caring what it costs. 9 — I'm not choosing words anymore. 10 — I don't fully remember it afterward.

Most people can only detect 8 and up. Everything below it reads as "fine." That's the whole problem — by the time you notice, you're past the point where noticing helps.

So the training is detection, not control. Three times a day, stop and ask: what number am I at right now? Most of the time the answer is a 2 and it feels like a waste of time. It isn't. You're building the instrument. Once you can reliably feel a 4, you get to act at a 4 — and at a 4 you still have every tool available to you.

The rule that follows: **your exit happens at 6.** Not 8. Six is the last rung where leaving is still a decision instead of a storm-out.
items.action: Write your own 1-10 ladder with a physical marker for each rung. Then check your number three times today.
items.reflection: What number were you at the last time you thought you were fine?

items.title: The Exit
items.content:
Everyone who beats this has the same tool, and it's not a clever phrase. It's a door.

The rule: at a 6, you leave the room. Not to win, not to punish, not to slam anything. You go, you come back. And it only works if it's built in advance, because at a 6 you are not designing anything.

Build it now, in four parts. **The sentence** — one line, agreed in advance, said flat: "I'm at a six. I need twenty minutes." That's it. No parting shot as you walk out, because a parting shot converts your exit into an attack. **The place** — decided ahead of time. Outside, the garage, around the block. Not the car if driving angry is one of your patterns. **The time** — twenty minutes minimum, an hour maximum, and you say which. **The return** — non-negotiable. You come back, and you come back to finish the conversation. 

That last part is what separates a time-out from abandonment. If you leave and don't come back, or come back and act like it never happened, they don't experience safety — they experience being walked out on, and next time they'll rush to placate you before you can go. Now your exit is a threat.

And what you do in those twenty minutes matters. Walking helps. Cold water helps. Rehearsing your case does not — that's feeding it. If you come back hotter than you left, you spent the whole time arguing with someone who wasn't there.

Tell the people you live with about this today, while you're calm. It works far better as something they're expecting than as something you spring on them mid-fight.
items.action: Write your four parts down: the sentence, the place, the time, the return. Then tell your household — today, calm, out loud.
items.reflection: When you've walked out before, did you come back and finish it? Or did it just get buried?

items.title: HALT: The Boring Half Of The Work
items.content:
Hungry. Angry. Lonely. Tired. It sounds like a fridge magnet and it's the most reliable predictor of your worst days.

Go back through your last five blowups and check them against it. Most people find at least two boxes ticked every single time. Skipped lunch. Four hours of sleep. Haven't had a real conversation with anyone in a week. Already been carrying something since morning. The trigger got the blame, but the trigger walked into a house where the gas was already leaking.

This is unglamorous and it is most of the win. You cannot white-knuckle self-control on four hours of sleep — restraint is the first thing a short night takes from most people, as anyone who's tried it knows. That's an empty tank, not weakness. Same with food: running on nothing makes everything read as a threat.

So three unimpressive commitments do more for your temper than any amount of resolve. Eat at roughly the same times, every day. Protect sleep like it's medical, because it is. And have at least one real conversation a week with somebody who isn't in your house — isolation makes everything heavier, and most of us are catastrophically bad at this one.

The fourth letter is the one you're already working. But you'll work it far better rested and fed.
items.action: Check the last five times you lost it against H-A-L-T. Count the boxes. Then fix the one that shows up most.
items.reflection: Which letter is chronically true for you — not occasionally, but as your normal condition?

items.title: How Your Other Habits Feed This One
items.content:
If you're working more than one thing in this app, they aren't separate problems. They're the same problem wearing different clothes, and they feed each other in a loop.

Alcohol does it most directly — it takes the brakes off exactly the system you're trying to strengthen, which is why so many of the worst nights involve it. But it's not just drink. Porn and compulsive sex run a crash on the back end: shame, self-disgust, and nothing left in the tank, which leaves you primed to detonate over something small an hour later. Binge eating does the same. Gambling adds money panic and secrecy on top. Overwork means you arrive home already empty, every day, with nothing left for the people who get you last.

And it runs the other way too. After you blow up, what do you reach for? For a lot of people the answer is the other addiction — because the shame from the outburst is exactly the feeling the habit was always there to numb. Rage feeds the habit, the habit feeds the rage, round and round, and each lap makes the next one easier.

Which is why working them one at a time in isolation so often stalls. Progress on the anger will collapse if the drinking stays, and the drinking will keep pulling you back if the shame from the outbursts never gets addressed.

In this app, add both as focus areas so you're actually looking at the loop instead of one arc of it.
items.action: In Profile → Your focus areas, make sure everything you're actually fighting is on the list. Then write one sentence on how two of them feed each other for you.
items.reflection: Which comes first for you — does the habit follow the rage, or does the rage follow the habit?

items.title: Sleep And The Short Fuse
items.content:
One short night takes a visible chunk off your patience — anyone who has worked a double or parented a newborn already knows. Under-slept people snap harder at smaller things and take longer to come down. You've proven it on yourself a hundred Tuesdays in a row: short sleep, short fuse.

Which means when you're running on five hours, restraint isn't just harder, it's running on fumes. Not an excuse — you're still responsible for what you do — but it does tell you where to aim. It is far easier to protect a bedtime than to summon superhuman patience at 6pm with nothing in the tank.

The usual things, and they work: a fixed time you stop, most nights, including weekends. No screen in the last thirty minutes, because that's the window where you scroll yourself into fresh outrage right before trying to sleep. Alcohol tends to wreck the back half of the night even when it knocks you out. Caffeine after mid-afternoon can still be with you at bedtime. And if you're lying there running arguments — Day 14 is about exactly that, and it's the biggest sleep thief of all for angry people.

If you snore heavily and wake up unrefreshed no matter how long you're in bed, get checked for sleep apnea. Untreated apnea can leave you chronically irritable and exhausted, and it's very treatable. More than a few "bad tempers" have turned out to be a sleep problem.
items.action: Set one fixed bedtime and hold it every night this week, including the weekend. Track your worst moment each day next to it.
items.reflection: What's your honest average? And what would a week of an extra hour actually change?

items.title: Rehearsing: Building The Case
items.content:
Here's the habit that keeps your fuse permanently short, and it doesn't happen during the fight. It happens in the shower, in the truck, at 2am.

You replay it. You add the line you should have said. You imagine their face when you say it. You assemble the evidence — the pattern, the other times, what it proves about them. It feels productive, like preparing. It is the opposite of preparing. Every pass re-runs the same surge as the original event, so you're getting angry at something that's over, on a loop, for free.

Worse, you're building a case. Each rehearsal makes the story cleaner and them guiltier, until by the time the real conversation happens you're not responding to what they just said — you're delivering a verdict you wrote three days ago, with evidence they didn't know was being collected. That's why these blowups feel so out of proportion from the outside. They're the summation of a trial nobody told them they were in.

Rumination isn't thinking. Thinking reaches a conclusion. Rumination goes in circles and its only product is heat.

Breaking it takes something physical, because you can't out-think a thought loop. Name it out loud — "I'm rehearsing" — and then change your body: get up, go outside, cold water, put music on, call someone. If it's a genuine problem that needs solving, write down the one specific thing you'll say and then stop. The written sentence gives the loop somewhere to land.
items.action: Catch yourself rehearsing once today. Say "I'm rehearsing" out loud and change what your body is doing within ten seconds.
items.reflection: How many hours a week do you spend in imaginary arguments? What has any of it ever actually solved?

items.title: The Line: Anger Versus Control
items.content:
Two weeks in, this is the lesson that matters most, and it's the one nobody wants. Read it slowly and answer honestly, because the answer changes what you should be doing.

**Anger** is an emotion you have. It's dysregulated, it's disproportionate, it goes off in front of the wrong people — and it's mostly about your own poor regulation.

**Control** is a pattern of behavior aimed at another person: making them smaller, more compliant, more afraid, more dependent. It doesn't require a raised hand. Monitoring where they are. Deciding who they can see. Holding the money. Punishing with silence for days. Making them account for every purchase. Ending every complaint by putting them on trial. Keeping them so unsure of your mood that they stop asking for things.

Here's the test, and it's brutal because it works. **Does it happen with everyone, or mostly with one person?** If you truly cannot regulate, it comes out at your boss, your mother, the police officer, the person at the counter. If you hold it together all day and it only comes apart on one person behind a closed door — that isn't a broken switch. That's a choice about who's safe to do it to.

Second test: **has their world gotten smaller since you've been together?** Fewer friends, less money of their own, less freedom to come and go. Anger doesn't shrink somebody's life. Control does.

If the honest answer is that it's mostly one person, and their world has narrowed, then what you have is not a temper problem and this track alone won't fix it. Day 28 covers what actually does. Reading that is not admitting you're a monster. It's the first genuinely honest thing available to you.
items.action: Answer both tests in writing. Everyone, or mostly one person? Has their world gotten bigger or smaller? Don't soften it.
items.reflection: If they were asked privately whether they feel free in this house, what would they say?

items.title: What Fear Does To A Room
items.content:
You can do enormous damage without ever touching anyone, and most people in this position genuinely do not know it's happening — because from the inside, it looks like nothing happened.

The punch to the wall instead of the person. The door. The plate. Standing up and stepping in close. Going very quiet and very still. The look. Driving fast with them in the car while you're angry. Throwing the phone. None of it leaves a mark, and every one of it teaches the same lesson: *they could, and the only thing stopping them is their mood.*

That lesson doesn't wear off between incidents. Once it's learned, it's in the room permanently. Every disagreement after that is conducted by someone doing risk assessment. When they back down, you don't win an argument — you get compliance from someone who is calculating. And you may not even be able to tell the difference, which is exactly why people keep doing it while sincerely believing things are fine.

The children learn faster than anyone. They don't need to be hit and they don't need to be in the room. They learn to read a face from across a house and to be very quiet in a way you might have mistaken for being well-behaved.

What this means for the work: "I've never laid a hand on anyone" is not the standard. The standard is whether the people in your house can disagree with you without doing a risk calculation first. If they can't, punching a wall counted.
items.action: List every non-touching thing you've done while angry — the wall, the door, the object, the standing over. Look at the list without arguing with it.
items.reflection: When they back down, is it because you're right — or because it's not worth what it costs?

items.title: If You Have Put Hands On Someone
items.content:
No softening on this one.

If you have grabbed, shoved, pinned, blocked a doorway, taken keys or a phone so they couldn't leave, cornered someone, or put a hand anywhere near a throat — that is physical abuse. Once counts. Whether or not it left a mark, whether or not you'd been drinking, whether or not they hit back, whether or not you were provoked. There is no version of the story where it becomes something else.

And one specific thing, because most people do not know it: any hand on the neck, even briefly, even with no bruise, is one of the strongest known predictors of a partner later being killed. If that has ever happened, you are not dealing with a temper. You are at a point that requires professional intervention now, not a thirty-day track.

Here's what people do instead, and you'll recognize it. Minimize — it was only the once, I only grabbed their arm. Contextualize — you don't know what they'd said. Trade — they hit me too. Every one of those is a way to stay the same person. 

What accountability actually looks like: you say the specific thing you did, with no sentence attached explaining why. "I grabbed you by the arms and pushed you into the wall." Not "things got physical." Not "we had a rough night." The exact action, owned in the first person.

Then you get real help, which is Day 28. If you do only one thing from this entire track, make it that one. This is past what an app can carry.

And if you're afraid you're going to hurt someone tonight — leave the house now, and call 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, which handles all crises, not only suicide). Leaving is not weakness. It's the only useful thing available to you at that moment.
items.action: If it's happened, write the sentence: the specific action, first person, no explanation attached. Then read Day 28 today rather than in eleven days.
items.reflection: What words have you been using to describe it that make it smaller than it was?

items.title: The Words That Don't Come Back
items.content:
People who'd never raise a hand will say things in eight seconds that outlast a bruise by twenty years, and then wonder why they're still bringing up something from 2011.

The reason those specific sentences land so hard is that you aimed them. You know their weak spot — their body, their family, their failures, the thing they told you in confidence at 2am when they trusted you. In a rage you reach for the most effective thing available, and the most effective thing is always the one they gave you when they felt safe. That's the part that does the lasting damage: not the volume, the betrayal of what they'd handed you.

"I didn't mean it, I was angry" is the standard defense and it's mostly false. You may not have meant it as a settled belief. But you found it, chose it, and deployed it because you knew it would hurt. That's aim, not accident.

And unlike a broken door, there's nothing to repair or replace. The sentence is now permanently in their head, in your voice. Every time you're heated afterward, they hear it coming. That's why they flinch at a tone that seems like nothing to you.

The defense against this is specific and it works: **the things they told you in confidence are permanently off the table.** Not off the table when you're calm — off the table, period, as a category, decided now while you're not angry. It's much easier to hold a rule you set in advance than to make a judgment call at an 8.
items.action: Write the worst thing you've ever said to someone you love. Then write the rule: what is permanently off the table from now on.
items.reflection: What sentence of yours do they still carry? Do you already know what it is?

items.title: The House Your Kids Are Learning In
items.content:
If there are children in the house, they are not bystanders, and they don't need to have seen anything to have been shaped by it.

They hear it through the wall. They read the silence at breakfast. They watch a parent's face to find out what kind of day it's going to be, and they get good at it — that skill, hypervigilance, can follow them into classrooms, jobs and relationships thirty years from now. Kids in homes like this often carry more anxiety, more trouble sleeping and concentrating, more stomach aches with no clear cause. They also learn, without a word being said, one of two roles: the one who explodes, or the one who puts up with it. Then they carry it into their own house.

And there's the specific damage of being made responsible for it. Kids in eggshell houses become managers — keeping the peace, keeping the other one quiet, being perfect so it doesn't start. That's a job, and it's not theirs.

Here's what changes it, and it's more available than you'd think: children tend to do far better when the adult owns it. Not a lecture, not a promise, not tears that make them comfort you. Something plain, at their level: "I yelled last night. That was my fault, not yours, and it isn't your job to fix it. I'm working on it." That one sentence takes the weight of responsibility off a child who has been carrying it silently.

They don't need you to have been perfect. They need to know it wasn't them.
items.action: If they saw or heard the last one, tell them the plain version today: it was mine, it wasn't yours, I'm working on it. No speech.
items.reflection: What is your child learning about how adults handle being upset? Would you want them repeating it in their own house?

items.title: The Excuses, Named
items.content:
Say them all out loud today, so they stop working on you in the dark.

*"They know exactly how to push my buttons."* Maybe. They're still your buttons, and nobody else in your life gets to press them and get this.

*"I only get like that when I'm stressed."* Stress explains why it's more likely. It doesn't choose the target, and it doesn't pick which words to use.

*"It was worse in the house I grew up in."* Probably true, and completely beside the point. The bar isn't your childhood home. Your kids don't get a comparison, they only get you.

*"I'd been drinking."* You chose to drink knowing exactly what you're like. That's not a defense, it's an additional decision.

*"At least I've never hit anyone."* Not the standard. Day 16.

*"They're overreacting."* If somebody's response to you seems wildly out of proportion, they're probably not responding only to today. They're responding to the accumulated file.

*"I apologized."* Apologies are not currency you can spend on the next one. If the same apology has been required more than twice, it's stopped being an apology and become part of the pattern.

*"That's just who I am."* It's who you've been. It's not a diagnosis and it's not fixed.

Every one of these is a way to keep the behavior and dodge the reckoning. Watch which one you reach for first — that's the load-bearing one, and it's the one to knock out.
items.action: Write down the one you use most. Then, underneath, write what would actually be true instead.
items.reflection: Who in your life still accepts your favorite excuse? Do you rely on that?

items.title: Accountability Without Self-Hatred
items.content:
Three weeks in, and this is the balance point the whole thing turns on.

You've now looked at things you'd rather not have looked at. Two exits are open and both are comfortable. One is to minimize — I've done the work, they should move on now. The other is to collapse — I'm the villain, look at all of it, what's the point. Both end the work. The collapse is the sneakier one because it feels like remorse.

Watch what self-hatred actually does in a house. It makes you fragile, so nobody can raise anything without you falling apart, which means they stop raising things — and now your remorse is doing the same job your anger did: keeping them quiet. It makes them comfort you about the thing you did to them. And it gives you an exit ramp: someone who's garbage can't be expected to change.

Real accountability is much less dramatic than that. It's specific rather than global — *I did this thing on Tuesday*, not *I'm a terrible person*. It's steady rather than intense — the same work on the day you don't feel it. It's measured in what other people experience, not in how bad you feel. And it doesn't require them to comfort you or forgive you on any schedule.

The simplest test: after you own something, does the other person feel lighter or heavier? If your accountability leaves them carrying more, it wasn't accountability. It was another delivery of your feelings.

Week four is repair.
items.action: Take the biggest thing you've named this month. Write the specific version — the action, the date, the person. Not the global verdict about yourself.
items.reflection: When you own something, who ends up being comforted?

items.title: A Real Apology
items.content:
Most apologies from angry people are not apologies. They're requests — for the mood to end, for the subject to close, for reassurance that you're not a bad person.

The fakes, by name. "I'm sorry you felt that way" — blames their reaction. "I'm sorry, but you know what you'd said" — everything before *but* is deleted. "I said sorry, what more do you want" — that's a demand. And the loudest one: "I'm sorry, I'm a piece of garbage, I don't deserve you" — now they're managing your feelings about the thing you did to them.

A real one has four parts and no fifth part.

**Name it exactly.** "I yelled at you in front of the kids and I called you stupid." Not "last night." Not "how I've been." The specific action.

**Name the effect, without softening it.** "You were scared of me in your own house, and the kids saw it."

**No explanation attached.** No *because*, no *I'd had a rough day*. Reasons belong in a conversation about the pattern, at a calm time. Inside an apology, a reason is always a defense.

**Say what changes, concretely.** "When I get to a six I'm leaving the room for twenty minutes and coming back." Something they can watch you do.

Then the part almost everyone gets wrong: **you stop, and you don't ask for anything.** Not forgiveness, not reassurance, not "are we okay." You said it, you meant it, you go and do the thing. Their response is theirs.
items.action: Write out a real one for the most recent incident, all four parts, nothing attached. Read it back and delete every "because."
items.reflection: How many of your apologies have ended with you being reassured?

items.title: You Don't Set The Clock On Repair
items.content:
Here's where a lot of people get angry all over again, about the very process of getting better.

You've been doing the work for a few weeks. You haven't blown up. You apologized properly. And they're still guarded — still watchful, still bringing up old things, still not warm. And something in you says: *I'm trying, what more do they want, this isn't fair.* That resentment, unexamined, is what ends most attempts at this.

So understand what you're asking. Trust isn't a decision they're withholding out of spite; it's a prediction they make from evidence, and yours has years of evidence on one side and weeks on the other. That prediction is not going to flip on your timetable. The watchfulness you're seeing isn't punishment. It's a well-calibrated instrument doing its job.

And the maths is lopsided in a way that feels unjust and simply is the case: it took a long time to build and it takes a long time to unbuild, and one bad night sets it back further than ten good weeks moved it forward. That's not them being unfair. That seems to be how it works in every human being.

Which means: no scoreboard, no deadline, no "I've been good for three months." You stop keeping count. You just become someone different and let the evidence accumulate at whatever rate it accumulates. And if they never fully come back — that's a possible outcome, and doing it anyway is the whole test of whether the change was for them or for the credit.
items.action: Notice the next time you feel owed something for the work. Don't say it. Write it down instead, and look at what you were expecting.
items.reflection: Are you changing because you want to be different, or because you want it acknowledged?

items.title: Say It At Three, Not At Eight
items.content:
Here's a pattern that explains most of the explosions that seem to come from nowhere.

You don't mention it. It's small, you don't want to be difficult, you're not a complainer. So it goes in the bag. Something else goes in the bag. Then something else. You carry that bag for two weeks being reasonable, and then someone leaves a cup out and the entire bag comes out at once — two weeks of grievances delivered in ninety seconds by someone who is, from their point of view, losing their mind about a cup.

That's not a temper problem. That's a communication problem that becomes a temper problem. And it comes from a belief a lot of us carry without examining it: that saying what I need is weakness, or nagging, or something you should just handle quietly. So you stay silent right up until you're not, and the only volume you've got left is the one that frightens people.

The fix is small and it feels awkward for about a month. Say it at a 3. "I need twenty minutes when I get in before anyone asks me anything." "When plans change without telling me, it gets to me — can we text about it?" Flat, early, specific, no case attached because there's no case yet.

It feels petty. It feels like making a thing out of nothing. That's precisely the point: at a 3 it *is* nothing, and it can be handled like nothing. The same sentence at an 8 is a fight.

Emptying the bag weekly is most of what stops the bag from ever being thrown.
items.action: Name one thing currently in the bag. Say it out loud today, calm and specific, before it grows.
items.reflection: What have you been carrying for weeks that you could have said in one sentence on day one?

items.title: Assertive Is Not Aggressive
items.content:
A lot of us think there are two settings: swallow it, or go off. Passive or aggressive. Doormat or explosion. And because being a doormat is unbearable, they pick the explosion and call it standing up for themselves.

There's a third setting, and it's the one most of us were never shown. Assertive means saying the hard thing directly, without heat, without an attack, and without needing the other person to agree in order for you to be alright.

The difference is not volume, it's aim. Aggressive goes at the person — you always, you never, what's wrong with you. Assertive goes at the thing — here's what happened, here's the effect on me, here's what I'm asking for. The format is boring and it works: *when X happens, I feel Y, and I'm asking for Z.*

And here's the part that surprises people: assertive is more powerful than aggressive, not less. Aggression gets compliance and costs you respect — people manage you, wait you out, tell you what you want to hear. Someone who says the hard thing calmly and doesn't blink is much harder to dismiss. You've probably met one. You probably took them seriously.

The test of whether you're actually assertive rather than aggressive-in-a-quieter-voice: can you say the thing, have them disagree, and be alright? If their disagreement escalates you, you weren't being assertive — you were issuing a demand and calling it communication.
items.action: Take a conflict you're avoiding. Write it as: when X happens, I feel Y, I'm asking for Z. Then say it that way.
items.reflection: Who do you know who says hard things calmly? What does that get them that shouting has never got you?

items.title: The Ones Still Here
items.content:
Somebody stayed. However battered it is, somebody is still in the house, still answering the phone, still giving you a chance you may or may not have earned. Start there, because rebuilding with the people still present is more available than anything else in this track.

What rebuilds trust is not intensity. It isn't the big conversation, the grand gesture, the emotional night where everything gets said. Those feel enormous to you and change almost nothing for them, because they've seen big nights before and watched what followed. What changes things is small, boring, repeated evidence: you said twenty minutes and you came back in twenty minutes. You said you'd handle it and you handled it. They raised something difficult and nothing happened.

That last one is the real currency. Every time somebody tells you something you don't want to hear and the room stays safe, a little of the calculation comes out of them. That's the mechanism. Not apologies — safety, demonstrated, repeatedly, especially when it's inconvenient.

One concrete thing: get curious about the ordinary parts of their life again. What are they worried about at work, what did they do today. People in this pattern often stopped asking years ago, because everything narrowed down to managing the tension. Being asked an ordinary question by somebody who actually wants the answer is, for a person who has been walking on eggshells, unusually loud evidence that the weather has changed.

And let them have their pace. They may test it. That's not disloyalty, it's due diligence.
items.action: Ask someone in your house an ordinary question about their day, and listen to the whole answer without steering it anywhere.
items.reflection: When did you last hear about their day without it being about the household or about you?

items.title: The Ones Who Left
items.content:
Some of them are gone. And you might not have understood how much it cost them until there was nobody left to tell.

This is its own grief and it doesn't get much sympathy, because you caused it. But it's real, and unprocessed it turns into two things that will drag you back: bitterness — they left, after everything, after I was working on it — or a self-hatred so total it becomes an excuse to stop trying.

A few honest things about it.

You probably don't get to fix it. Reaching out is very often about relieving your own guilt rather than serving them, and for many people the message itself is another intrusion. If there's any chance the contact would frighten them, or if you were told not to, don't. Wanting to apologize does not entitle you to their attention.

What you can do is carry it forward rather than around. The cost of what happened is the most powerful reason you have not to build the same house twice. Not as punishment — as information you paid a lot for.

And if a genuine amends ever becomes possible — invited, on their terms, at a time they choose — the rule is the same as Day 22: name it exactly, no explanation attached, ask for nothing. Amends is not a request to be released.

Until then, the useful move is to let the loss make you different rather than let it make you bitter. That's the only version of this that honours what it cost them.
items.action: Write the letter you'd send if it were welcome. Then don't send it — put it in the app's Journal. It was for you.
items.reflection: Are you carrying this as information, or as resentment?

items.title: When An App Is Not Enough
items.content:
Straight talk about the limits of what you're holding in your hand.

This track can teach you the mechanics, the ladder, the exit, and how to apologize properly. Plenty of people get real, durable results from exactly that. But there are situations where continuing to work this alone is a way of avoiding the thing that would actually help, and you should know what they are.

**Get professional help now if:** you have ever been physical, once counts. Anything involving a throat. You've frightened a child. It's mostly one person behind a closed door (Day 15). Weapons have ever been part of it. Or you've been at this a while and nothing is moving.

**What to ask for.** For anger that's genuinely about regulation: a therapist who does CBT for anger, or a group anger-management program. But if what you've got is the pattern in Day 15 — control, not just temper — anger management is the wrong tool and can even make it worse by giving you better language for the same behavior. The right one is a certified **Batterer Intervention Program** (also called an Abusive Partner Intervention Program). They exist in most US states, many take self-referrals rather than only court orders, and they are the thing built specifically for this. Ask your county's domestic violence agency for the certified list.

**One caution.** Couples counseling is not the right room when abuse is present. It treats the problem as shared, and it puts your partner in a position where honesty can cost them later. Do your own work in your own room first.

**Two numbers.** 988 — Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, call or text, for any crisis including "I'm about to do something." 1-800-799-7233 — the National Domestic Violence Hotline, which also takes calls from people who want to stop being abusive and will point you toward local programs.

Making that call is not surrendering your self-respect. It's the first thing in years that someone in your position can do that actually works.
items.action: Find one real option today — a local program's number or a therapist who lists anger. Write it down. Calling can be tomorrow.
items.reflection: What's the actual reason you haven't done this yet? Say the real one, not the schedule.

items.title: Your Plan For The Bad Night
items.content:
There will be a bad night. Not maybe. Something will stack up — no sleep, bad news, money, an old trigger on a day you had nothing left — and you'll be at an 8 before you've registered climbing. People who beat this are not people who stopped getting angry. They're the ones who had a plan written down before they needed it.

Write yours today, while you're calm, because at an 8 you will not design anything. Six parts:

**My early warnings** — the physical ones from Day 9. What a 5 actually feels like in my body.

**My exit** — the sentence, the place, the time, the return. Word for word.

**My twenty minutes** — what I actually do: walk, cold water, long exhale. What I do not do: rehearse, drink, drive, get on the phone.

**My person** — one name and number. Someone I text the word "bad" to. No explanation required, just sent.

**My line** — the thing that means this is bigger than a bad night and I call the number from Day 28 tomorrow, not eventually.

**My repair** — what I do in the morning if I blew it. Day 22, all four parts, no fifth.

And one rule that covers most of the damage: **no decisions and no conversations at an 8.** Nothing said at an 8 has ever improved a situation. It can all wait until morning, and it will look different in the morning.

Put this in the app's Journal where you can actually reach it. A plan you can't find at 11pm isn't a plan.
items.action: Write all six parts into the Journal now. Then tell one person in your house that the plan exists and what the sentence is.
items.reflection: Where does it usually start for you? Where in that chain could you have stepped out?

items.title: The Person They Can Relax Around
items.content:
Thirty days ago you opened the hardest track in this app — the one about what you've done to other people rather than to yourself. Most people never open that door at all. They go their whole lives calling it a temper.

Here's what you have now that you didn't have a month ago. You know anger is almost never the first feeling. You know the surge tends to pass in about ninety seconds if you stop feeding it. You know your triggers and your ladder, and you know your exit happens at 6, not 8. You know the difference between a temper and a pattern of control, and you answered that question honestly. You know what a real apology is, and that it ends without asking for anything. And you know the two numbers to call when it's past what you can hold alone.

What you're aiming for isn't a person who never gets angry — that person doesn't exist and wouldn't be much use. It's something more specific: **someone the people in their house can relax around.** Somebody who can be told bad news. Who can be disagreed with without anyone doing the maths first. Whose mood isn't the weather everyone else has to plan their day around.

That's the whole target. Not perfection — predictability. Being safe to be honest with. It sounds small next to the size of what you've been carrying. It's the thing your family has wanted for years and never asked for out loud.

Go back to any lesson you need. Keep the plan where you can reach it. Keep the exit sentence, and keep coming back after twenty minutes.

The person they can relax around is built on ordinary days, one at a time. Same as everything else in here.
items.action: Read your plan from Day 29 once more. Then go do one ordinary, unannounced thing for someone you've been hard on.
items.reflection: One year from now, what do you want the people in your house to say has changed?
